archetype.name: Bubble Team (special-teams driven)
archetype.definition: A .500 club whose good power play and penalty kill cover for a roster that is slightly out-chanced at 5-on-5, leaving it in the middle of the Central race with no margin to spare.

report.headline: Even goal differential, better special teams and a goalie question the stopwatch hasn't answered
report.take:
St. Louis is a perfectly balanced 5-5-1 team in the most literal sense: 35 goals scored, 35 allowed, a Goal Diff / GP of 0 that ranks 17th, and an 82-point pace. The site has them 20th, which fits. This is a middle-of-the-league roster with C grades at forward and on the blueline. Without a clear edge at even strength, it relies on its special units and on whichever goalie is in net.

The real change from last season is on special teams. The PP % has gone from .176 to .241 (10th), and the PK % from .767 to .828 (also 10th). Both are well above the league averages of .212 and .783. That is a big part of why a team that ranked 24th on offense a year ago now scores at a league-average clip (3.18 a game, 14th). At 5-on-5 the picture is plainer. CF % sits at exactly .500, and xGF % is .486, 20th. The Blues get their share of the puck but not quite their share of the good chances, and they give up 28.3 shots a game, 22nd.

The goaltending split is the biggest hidden story. Joel Hofer has a .917 Save % and +3.2 GSAx over 8 starts, ninth on the goalie tab. Jordan Binnington has an .831 and -5 GSAx in 3 starts, 65th of 69. The team's -1.2 Goalies GSAx is almost entirely Binnington's three nights, and the B goaltending grade reflects the starts weighting toward Hofer. Luck has also cut against them. The 98.1 5-on-5 PDO is below average, and Pts vs Goal Diff of -1.3 ranks 27th, with a one-goal loss in Minnesota and an overtime loss to San Jose among the defeats. On that evidence the record is, if anything, a touch worse than the play.

The flip side is that the play isn't very good either. The last five games went 2-3-0 with a -3 differential. The defense also gives up the most production to opposing centers of nearly any team, ranking 31st against that position. A team that leans on its power play and one hot goalie is a bubble team. Last year's 86 points were built on the opposite luck: Pts vs Goal Diff was +2.8 that season, with a negative goal differential. This year's group is a little better underneath, but not by enough to be called a playoff team yet.

strengths.title: Special teams transformed from last year
strengths.body: Both units rank 10th and sit comfortably above league average, a sharp turn from a .176 power play and .767 kill a year ago. With a forward group that spreads PP points around and no single shooter carrying it, the power play looks structurally better rather than a one-man hot streak. Eleven games is a thin sample for special teams, so some give-back is likely, but the improvement is large enough that some of it should hold.

strengths.title: Hofer is playing like a starter
strengths.body: Hofer's .917 Save % and +3.2 GSAx rank him ninth among goalies on the site, and he has taken most of the starts. His 2.4 GAA came behind a team that allows above-average shot volume, so the work is real rather than sheltered. If he keeps the crease, the team's goals-against rank of 15th should improve.

strengths.title: McTavish and the young wingers scoring
strengths.body: Mason McTavish leads the forwards with a 10.2 Game Score, 6 goals and 31 shots, and that volume says his production is earned. Jimmy Snuggerud also has 6 goals, on a smaller shot count that hints at some shooting luck. Dylan Holloway's 10 points round out a top group that is outproducing Robert Thomas so far.

concerns.title: Slightly out-chanced at 5-on-5
concerns.body: A .486 xGF % ranks 20th, and the 28.3 shots allowed a game rank 22nd. The Blues hold even possession but concede the better looks. That is the profile of a team that needs special teams and goaltending to stay at .500, and it is the part of the record least likely to fix itself.

concerns.title: Opposing centers are feasting
concerns.body: Opponents' centers have produced well above their own averages against St. Louis, ranking 31st, and they take a far larger share of the points against than the league norm. The blueline's heavy-minute pairs show it. Cam Fowler, Colton Parayko and Brandon Carlo all sit deep down the defense tab with negative +/- marks, while the better results come from Adam Jiricek and Justin Barron in lighter roles.

concerns.title: Binnington's starts are costing games
concerns.body: In three starts Binnington has an .831 Save % and -5 GSAx, which by itself turns a good goaltending season into a below-average one for the team. Three starts is far too few to judge him for the year. Still, every start he makes right now is a clear downgrade from Hofer.

trend.note: The season has swung between lopsided results, from a 1-6 opener in Colorado to 7-2 in Ottawa and 6-2 over Vegas, with no streak longer than three. The last five games (2-3-0, -3) lean slightly the wrong way, ending with a 0-4 shutout loss to Carolina.

weekAhead.headline: Boston and a stingy Rangers kill headline a hard four-game week
weekAhead.body:
Two home games open the week: Montréal (10th on the site), then Boston, the site's No. 1 team. The Blues then travel to Detroit and New York. The Bruins are the real test. They lead the league in Goal Diff / GP and Goalies GSAx, and their defense ranks second at holding opposing forwards under their averages. Their 107.6 PDO is the kind of number that fades, but probably not by Thursday. Montréal out-chances teams (.541 xGF %, 5th in CF %) but has the league's second-luckiest Pts vs Goal Diff and a power play ranked 28th. The Blues' penalty kill should have an edge there.

The road half splits two ways. Detroit is the softest opponent at 24th on the site, with a PK % of .658 (30th) that the St. Louis power play should attack. The Red Wings also out-shoot opponents, so it is no gimme. The Rangers are 9th, hold opposing centers second-best in the league, and kill 92.3% of penalties. That takes away exactly what St. Louis has leaned on. With no back-to-backs, Hofer can start most or all of the week, and that matters a lot here. A split of the four games would be a fair result.

keyMatchups.title: Blues power play vs Detroit's kill
keyMatchups.body: St. Louis' 10th-ranked power play meets a Detroit kill ranked 30th. This is the clearest edge of the week. With the Red Wings' skaters shooting just .085, special-teams goals could decide that game.

keyMatchups.title: Boston's finishing and goaltending
keyMatchups.body: Boston's 2nd-ranked Shooting % and Save % produce a league-best PDO. Their A+ forwards and goaltending grades suggest some of it is talent. St. Louis gives up shot volume, so it needs Hofer at his best and cannot afford a loose night defending the middle.

keyMatchups.title: Rangers' kill neutralizes the PP
keyMatchups.body: New York's .923 PK % ranks second, and its defense holds forwards well under their averages. The Blues will have to win at 5-on-5 at Madison Square Garden, which is where they have been weakest.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal against Boston and New York. Hofer's form is the difference between a split and a losing week.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying shape is a team a hair below even at 5-on-5, propped up by top-ten special teams and a starting goalie playing well above average. Some of that should regress, especially the special-teams percentages over a small sample. The close-game luck that has gone against them (27th in Pts vs Goal Diff) and a below-average 5-on-5 PDO should even out in their favor. Netting those out, the 82-point pace looks about right, with modest upside if Hofer keeps the job. Expect something in the 80-to-90 point range, which in a Central Division this bunched means fighting for a wild-card spot rather than holding one.

What would move them up is fixing the middle of the ice. The heavy-minute defense pairs and the goals conceded to centers are the clearest weakness. Giving more of those minutes to the better-performing Jiricek and Barron is the internal lever the numbers point to. What would sink them is the power play falling back toward last season's level while the 5-on-5 chance share stays in the 20s of the league ranking.
swingFactors: Hofer's share of starts and whether his save % holds
Power play sustaining a top-ten rate

confidence.note: Eleven games in. Special-teams and goalie numbers are small samples, and the goalie split rests on three Binnington starts.
